title: Ex-MP Somaiya Seeks Probe Into Sensex's Wild 2,200-Point Swing
excerpt: Former BJP MP Kirit Somaiya demands SEBI suspend its new Closing Auction Session mechanism after a five-minute crash and recovery on August 27.
body:
• Former BJP MP Kirit Somaiya has written to SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey demanding a temporary suspension of the Closing Auction Session (CAS) mechanism after the Sensex crashed over 2,200 points in five minutes on August 27.
  • The crash occurred during the first monthly derivatives expiry since CAS was introduced on August 3, exposing liquidity gaps when continuous trading halts at 3:15 PM.
  • Somaiya has called for a formal inquiry into whether the volatility was deliberate and has flagged liquidity fragmentation between parallel auctions on the NSE and BSE.
  • SEBI Chairman Pandey has stated the regulator is not considering immediate changes to the mechanism, comparing it to closing auction systems on the NYSE and LSE.

Five Minutes of Chaos on August 27

The BSE Sensex plunged over 2,200 points in a five-minute window on August 27, crashing from approximately 77,200 to below 75,000 between 3:18 PM and 3:23 PM IST, before recovering nearly 2,000 points by the time the auction settled. The index closed at 76,933.

The crash occurred during the first monthly derivatives expiry since the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) introduced its new Closing Auction Session (CAS) mechanism on August 3. CAS replaces the traditional 30-minute Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP) calculation with a single equilibrium-price auction designed to determine official closing prices.

As continuous trading in F&O-eligible stocks halted at 3:15 PM to make way for the auction process, liquidity appeared to vanish, triggering a cascade of sell orders. The severity of the move drew immediate attention: a viral post on social media noted that a ₹1 lakh investment in a 76,500 Sensex put option at 3:15 PM would have been worth ₹44 lakh by 3:20 PM.

Somaiya's Letter to SEBI

Former BJP MP Kirit Somaiya responded by writing to SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey on August 29, demanding both an inquiry and a temporary suspension of CAS. Somaiya urged the regulator not to treat the episode "casually" and raised the possibility that the sharp movement could have been deliberate.

"If the movement was the result of a weakness in the system, officials involved in designing the framework should explain what went wrong."

— Kirit Somaiya, former BJP MP, in letter to SEBI Chairman

At the heart of Somaiya's critique is what he calls a fundamental architectural flaw: the CAS framework halts continuous trading at 3:15 PM, removing deep market liquidity at precisely the moment when it is most critical. The auction mechanism then attempts to recreate adequate depth through a comparatively shallow order-collection process — a design Somaiya argues drains liquidity before trying to reconstitute it.

Liquidity Fragmentation Across Exchanges

Somaiya also flagged a separate structural concern. Under the current framework, the same security can undergo parallel closing auctions on the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE), each with independent order books. This can produce divergent equilibrium closing prices for the same stock — undermining the unified price discovery that CAS was designed to achieve.

Citing market observers, Somaiya noted that the absence of sufficient liquidity after 3:15 PM could systematically amplify volatility, as investors seeking to execute orders in that window face inadequate market depth. In a proposal attached to his letter, he called for CAS to be suspended immediately and redesigned based on practical market considerations before reintroduction.

SEBI Stands Firm

SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey stated on August 28 that the regulator is not considering any immediate changes to the CAS framework. He said the system is intended to bring Indian markets in line with closing auction mechanisms used on the New York Stock Exchange and the London Stock Exchange.

SEBI has already taken action against two firms — Copthall Mauritius Investment, an entity owned by JPMorgan Chase, and Mansi Share and Stock Broking — for alleged manipulation during an earlier weekly expiry on August 13. The regulator has indicated it expects volatility to subside as more brokers integrate CAS into their retail platforms and institutional participation increases.

"The MSCI rebalancing effective after markets close on August 31 would offer a key test, as passive-fund flows could lead to substantial order concentration."

— Niharika Tripathi, head of products and research, Wealthy.in

What It Means for Investors

For investors — including the large diaspora community with exposure to Indian equities — the August 27 episode is a warning about the risks of the new closing window. Under CAS, the "Last Traded Price" visible at 3:30 PM can differ significantly from the final settlement price announced after 3:35 PM. Market observers are advising traders to exercise caution during the 3:15 PM to 3:35 PM window, particularly on expiry days, as the absence of continuous matching can produce extreme slippage in options premiums.

Indian equity benchmarks posted a third consecutive weekly loss for the week ending August 29, their longest falling streak in five months. The Nifty 50 fell 0.3% for the week while the Sensex dropped 0.4%, with the CAS overhang continuing to weigh on sentiment. The MSCI rebalancing on August 31 will serve as the next major stress test for the mechanism.
